name: St John the Baptist's Church, Dronfield
text: Your train passes close to St John the Baptist's Church in Dronfield, on the train's {side}, which dates from the late 13th century. Its east window of 1887 was designed by F. R. Shields and highly praised by Edward Burne-Jones.

name: St Mary's Church, Melton Mowbray
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church in Melton Mowbray, on the train's {side}, the largest parish church in Leicestershire. It is built on a plan more usual for a cathedral, and is one of only five parish churches in the country with aisled transepts.

name: Shrewsbury Abbey
text: Your train passes close to Shrewsbury Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 1083 as a Benedictine monastery by Roger de Montgomery, Earl of Shrewsbury. Its nave survived the 16th century as a parish church, and the abbey is the setting of Ellis Peters's Cadfael mysteries.

name: Whittington Castle
text: Your train passes near Whittington Castle, on the train's {side}, a castle of the Welsh Marches on the English side of Offa's Dyke. Llywelyn ab Iorwerth of Gwynedd captured and destroyed it in 1223; it was rebuilt in stone, and an investigation in 2003 found that in the 14th century its outer bailey had held two elaborate gardens, surrounded by water.

name: Chirk Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Chirk Viaduct, 30 metres above the River Ceiriog, designed by Henry Robertson and built by Thomas Brassey between 1846 and 1848. The border between Wales and England runs across the viaduct at an angle, and beside it stands the Chirk Aqueduct, built in 1801.

name: Gay Meadow
text: Your train passes close to the site of Gay Meadow, on the train's {side}, home of Shrewsbury Town from 1910 to 2007, on the banks of the River Severn. For many years the coracle maker Fred Davies sat in his coracle during home matches, fetching stray footballs out of the river.

name: St Laurence's Church, Church Stretton
text: Your train passes near St Laurence's Church in Church Stretton, on the train's {side}, whose nave dates from the 12th century. Above its north doorway is a sheela na gig, a carved figure of a kind found on some medieval churches.

name: Shropshire Hills Discovery Centre
text: Your train passes near the Shropshire Hills Discovery Centre, on the train's {side}, a museum of the hills' history, geography and wildlife that opened in 2001. Its exhibition includes a life-sized model mammoth and an Iron Age roundhouse.

name: St Cuthbert's Church, Clungunford
text: Your train passes near St Cuthbert's Church at Clungunford, on the train's {side}, beside the River Clun. The village is named not after a ford but after Gunward, a Saxon lord who owned this part of the Clun valley: Domesday Book calls it Clone Gunward.

name: Coxall Knoll
text: Your train passes near Coxall Knoll, on the train's {side}, a hill on the border of Shropshire and Herefordshire with an Iron Age hillfort on its summit. Local tradition, Arthur Mee wrote, holds it to be the place of Caratacus's last stand against the Romans.

name: Bucknell motte
text: Your train passes near the motte at Bucknell, on the train's {side}, an earth mound that is all that remains of a Norman castle. It stands on the banks of the River Redlake, close to an old river crossing and the parish church.

name: Offa's Dyke near Nether Skyborry
text: Your train passes near a section of Offa's Dyke, on the train's {side}, the great earthwork named after Offa, king of Mercia in the eighth century. The border between England and Wales still mostly runs within a few miles of it.

name: Stokesay Castle
text: Your train passes close to Stokesay Castle, on the train's {side}, one of the finest surviving fortified manor houses in England. It was largely built in the late 13th century by Laurence of Ludlow, one of the leading wool merchants in England.

name: Leominster Priory
text: Your train passes near the Priory Church in Leominster, on the train's {side}, built for a Benedictine priory in about the 13th century, with a ducking stool on display inside. Its first eight bells, cast at Chepstow in 1755, came upstream by barge on the rivers Wye and Lugg.

name: Royal National College for the Blind
text: Your train passes near the Royal National College for the Blind, on the train's {side}, founded in London in 1872 and now in Hereford, for blind and partially sighted students aged 16 to 25. It has been home to the England blind football team.

name: Church of St Mary and St David, Kilpeck
text: Your train passes near the church at Kilpeck, on the train's {side}, built around 1140 and famous for its stone carvings. Nikolaus Pevsner called it one of the most perfect Norman churches in England.

name: Shrewsbury Flaxmill Maltings
text: Your train passes close to Shrewsbury Flaxmill Maltings, on the train's {side}, built as a flax mill in 1796 and 1797 to Charles Bage's design. It was the first iron-framed building in the world, and has been called "the grandfather of skyscrapers".

name: Shrewsbury Castle
text: Your train passes near Shrewsbury Castle, on the train's {side}, a red sandstone castle on the neck of land in the River Severn's loop where the town grew up. William the Conqueror ordered it in about 1067, and Roger de Montgomery greatly extended it as a base for campaigns into Wales.

name: Wombridge Priory
text: Your train passes near the site of Wombridge Priory, on the train's {side}, a small Augustinian monastery founded in the early 12th century by William of Hadley. It was never a large community, and was dissolved in 1536.

name: Telford Theatre
text: Your train passes near Telford Theatre, on the train's {side}, built on the site of the Great Western Nail Works and opened as Oakengates Town Hall in 1968. The jockey Sir Gordon Richards performed the opening.

name: St Andrew's Church, Shifnal
text: Your train passes near St Andrew's Church in Shifnal, on the train's {side}, which has a Norman chancel. It was once a minster with a chapter of priests serving the villages round about, until it was given to Shrewsbury Abbey around 1087.

name: Royal Air Force Museum Midlands
text: Your train passes near the Royal Air Force Museum Midlands, on the train's {side}, opened at RAF Cosford in 1979. Its rare aircraft include the second prototype of the TSR-2 and one of only two Vickers Wellingtons left in the world.

name: St Cuthbert's Church, Donington
text: Your train passes near St Cuthbert's Church at Donington, on the train's {side}, more than 900 years old and founded by Roger de Montgomery. Its old tower collapsed on March 25th 1879 and was rebuilt the following year.

name: Albrighton Moat
text: Your train passes near Albrighton Moat, on the train's {side}, a moat round a small platform of earth that held a manor house in the 13th or 14th century. A survey in 1990 found the remains of the main building and its porch, facing a causeway that linked it to the rest of the site.

name: Birches Bridge
text: Your train passes through Birches Bridge, on the train's {side}, an area of Codsall named after The Birches, a large estate first mentioned in court rolls of 1716. The station there was originally called Birches.

name: Grand Theatre, Wolverhampton
text: Your train passes near the Grand Theatre in Wolverhampton, on the train's {side}, designed by the theatre architect Charles J. Phipps and opened on December 10th 1894. It was not the town's first theatre, but it has outlasted its rivals.

name: Wolverhampton railway works
text: Your train passes the site of the Stafford Road Works, on the train's {side}, opened in 1849 and from 1854 the workshop of the Great Western Railway's Northern Division. It built some 800 locomotives until 1908, and repaired them until it closed in 1964.

name: St Michael and All Angels' Church, Penkridge
text: Your train passes close to St Michael and All Angels' Church in Penkridge, on the train's {side}, which has dominated the town since late Anglo-Saxon times. It was a collegiate church, and the nine clerics recorded there in Domesday Book served a wide area of Staffordshire.

name: Mill Meece Pumping Station
text: Your train passes close to Mill Meece Pumping Station, on the train's {side}, which began work in 1915, pumping water from boreholes for the Potteries. Two steam engines, fed by three Lancashire boilers, did the work; a preservation trust has restored it.

name: Izaak Walton's Cottage
text: Your train passes close to Izaak Walton's Cottage at Shallowford, on the train's {side}, a 17th-century timber-framed cottage that belonged to the author of The Compleat Angler. The railway, built through the valley in 1837, cut it off from part of the Meece, the brook whose fishing is thought to have drawn him there.

name: Bet365 Stadium
text: Your train passes near the bet365 Stadium, on the train's {side}, home of Stoke City since 1997. Sir Stanley Matthews opened it, and after his death in 2000 his ashes were buried beneath the centre circle.

name: Etruria Industrial Museum
text: Your train passes near the Etruria Industrial Museum, on the train's {side}, a bone and flint mill of 1857 that ground materials for the potteries, between the Trent and Mersey and Caldon canals. Fred Dibnah opened it as a museum in 1991.

name: Harecastle Tunnel
text: Your train passes near Harecastle Tunnel, on the train's {side}, which takes the Trent and Mersey Canal under Harecastle Hill. It is really two tunnels: James Brindley's of the late 18th century and Thomas Telford's of the late 1820s, which is the only one still open to boats.

name: Stoke Minster
text: Your train passes near Stoke Minster, on the train's {side}, on a site where the first church was built of timber in 670. Josiah Wedgwood and several generations of Josiah Spode's family are buried there.

name: Gladstone Pottery Museum
text: Your train passes near the Gladstone Pottery Museum, on the train's {side}, a coal-fired pottery of the kind once common in the area, saved from demolition in 1970. Its bottle ovens are among fewer than 50 left in Stoke-on-Trent.

name: Uttoxeter
text: Your train passes Uttoxeter, on the train's {side}, where Samuel Johnson's father ran a bookstall in the market. Young Samuel once refused to help on it; years later he stood in the rain without a hat as a penance, and the Johnson Memorial in the market place recalls it.

name: Uttoxeter Racecourse
text: Your train passes near Uttoxeter Racecourse, on the train's {side}, a National Hunt course built in 1907 by a company that took over the licence of Keele Park racecourse. The left-handed oval is a mile and two and a half furlongs round.

name: Essex Bridge
text: Your train passes near Essex Bridge, on the train's {side}, a packhorse bridge over the River Trent built in the late 16th century by the Earl of Essex, a favourite of Elizabeth I. Fourteen of its 40 arches remain, making it the longest surviving packhorse bridge in England.

name: Shugborough Tunnel
text: Your train goes through Shugborough Tunnel, 777 yards long, built in 1846 to hide the railway at the insistence of Thomas Anson, 1st Earl of Lichfield, who owned the Shugborough estate above it. Its two portals were designed by John Livock.

name: St Joseph and St Etheldreda, Rugeley
text: Your train passes near the Church of St Joseph and St Etheldreda in Rugeley, on the train's {side}, a Victorian Gothic church built in 1849 and 1850 as a major work of Charles Hansom. Its steeple was added to the west tower in 1868.
